title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context (§§36–48 of E555). Euler interpolates a curve through points whose abscissae form an 'interrupted' arithmetic progression, x = θω at ω = n, 1−n, 1+n, 2−n, 2+n, … (that is, k ± n). The interpolant is written with the nodal product, and its normalising constant Δ is a ratio of infinite products that Euler expresses through integrals of the type (p/q) := ∫_0^1 v^{p−1}(1−v^λ)^{(q−λ)/λ} dv. In modern notation (p/q) = (1/λ)B(p/λ, q/λ).

Corollary 1 (end of §45, top of this page). The identity proved on pp. 198–199 is λν((λ−μ)/ν)((λ−ν)/μ) = (ν/(μ−ν))·π sin((μ−ν)π/λ)/(sin(μπ/λ) sin(νπ/λ)). Put a = μ/λ, b = ν/λ and c = a − b. In modern form this reads b·B(1−a,b)·B(a,1−b) = bπ sin πc /(c sin πa sin πb). It follows from Γ(x)Γ(1−x) = π/sin πx together with Γ(1+c)Γ(1−c) = πc/sin πc. So a product of two such incomplete-looking integrals depends only on 'angles' (sines).

§46 (Corollary 2). Put n+ω = μ/λ, ω−n = ν/λ and z = v^λ in the original Δ. Then Δ = λ·∫v^{μ−1}(1−v^λ)^{−μ/λ}dv · ∫v^{μ−1}(1−v^λ)^{−ν/λ}dv : ∫v^{μ−1}(1−v^λ)^{−(μ−ν)/λ}dv. In Euler's symbol this is Δ = λ((λ−μ)/μ)((λ−ν)/μ)/((λ−μ+ν)/μ). By Corollary 1 it also equals νπ sin((μ−ν)π/λ)/((μ−ν) sin(μπ/λ) sin(νπ/λ)).

§47 (Corollary 3). Since ((λ−μ)/μ) = π/(λ sin μπ/λ), it follows that ((λ−ν)/μ)/((λ−μ+ν)/μ) = (ν/(μ−ν))·sin((μ−ν)π/λ)/sin(νπ/λ). Euler verifies this with the general theorem (q/p)/(r/p) = ((p+r)/q)/((p+q)/r). In Beta form this says Γ(q)Γ(p+r)/(Γ(p+q)Γ(r)) on both sides, so it is correct. The verification takes p = μ, q = λ−ν, r = λ−μ+ν. It then uses the reduction ((λ+ν)/(λ−ν)) = (ν/λ)(ν/(λ−ν)), its analogue for μ−ν, and the reflection values (ν/(λ−ν)) = π/(λ sin νπ/λ) and ((μ−ν)/(λ−μ+ν)) = π/(λ sin((μ−ν)π/λ)).

§48 (Exemplum 2). The data are alternating ordinates ±f at the nodes nθ, (1−n)θ, (1+n)θ, …. The general equation of §36 gives 2nΔy/(f(n−ω)) = Σ[1/(k+n−ω) + 1/(k+1−n−ω)] − (same with ω → −ω). Grouped as in §39, this equals π cot π(n−ω) − π cot π(n+ω) = π sin 2ωπ/(sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π). Substituting Δ = (n−ω)π sin 2nπ/(2n sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π) gives y = f sin 2ωπ/sin 2nπ = f sin(2πx/θ)/sin 2nπ. The interpolated curve is a sine curve.
errors: No genuine mathematical error found once the integrals are read correctly. If the machine transcription were taken literally (second integral v^{ν−1}, symbol ((λ−ν)/ν) in §§46–47), the stated equality Δ = νπ sin((μ−ν)π/λ)/((μ−ν) sin sin) would be false. Example: λ=4, μ=3, ν=1 gives a ratio off by Γ(b)Γ(a−b)/Γ(a)·(a−b) ≠ 1. With v^{μ−1} and ((λ−ν)/μ), which is the reading Euler's own verification on p. 201 requires (p = μ in the general theorem), everything checks.
Checked: Δ of §48 agrees with the Corollary 2 value under a = n+ω, b = ω−n. Also y = f sin 2ωπ/sin 2nπ reproduces +f, −f, +f at ω = n, 1−n, 1+n.

ideas.what: Notation (p/q) for ∫v^{p−1}(1−v^λ)^{q/λ−1}dv, symmetry (p/q) = (q/p), and the reduction (p/q) = (p−λ)/(p+q−λ)·((p−λ)/q)
ideas.modern_name: Beta function B(p/λ, q/λ)/λ and its recurrence
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Beta integrals); name 'Beta' due to Binet/Legendre
ideas.where_published: E321 'Observationes circa integralia formularum ∫x^{p−1}dx(1−x^n)^{q/n−1}…'; Institutiones calculi integralis

ideas.what: ((λ−p)/p) = π/(λ sin(pπ/λ)), used to reduce Δ to sines
ideas.modern_name: Euler reflection formula Γ(x)Γ(1−x) = π/sin πx
ideas.where_published: E321 and related papers on these integrals

ideas.modern_name: Beta product identity B(p,q)B(p+q,r) = B(p,r)B(p+r,q) (both equal Γ(p)Γ(q)Γ(r)/Γ(p+q+r))
ideas.where_published: E321 (fundamental theorem on products of these integrals)

ideas.what: Product of two Beta-type integrals ((λ−μ)/ν)((λ−ν)/μ) expressible purely by sines
ideas.modern_name: Consequence of reflection: Γ(1+c)Γ(1−c) = πc/sin πc
ideas.where_published: E555 itself; similar combinations in E321

ideas.what: Infinite interpolation through alternating data at nodes k±n gives the sine curve y = f sin(2πx/θ)/sin 2nπ, via π cot difference sums
ideas.modern_name: Infinite (Newton/Lagrange-type) interpolation on a union of two shifted lattices; partial-fraction expansion of cot
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for cot partial fractions; cardinal interpolation usually credited to E.T. Whittaker (1915)

missed.claim: Euler interpolates through samples at the symmetric two-lattice set {k ± n}. The nodal function is sin π(ω−n)·sin π(ω+n), and he obtains closed forms for the interpolant (a sine for alternating data, and on p. 203 non-uniqueness versus the uniform-lattice case). This is structurally the setting of 'second-order' or periodic nonuniform sampling (Kohlenberg 1953) and of uniqueness questions for entire interpolants. That literature does not, to my knowledge, cite Euler.
missed.quote: Sint applicatae, quae abscissis nθ, (1−n)θ, (1+n)θ, (2−n)θ, (2+n)θ, etc. respondent
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical precursor note for sampling/cardinal-interpolation history only. It is a connection of record, not a new theorem.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is correct Beta/Gamma manipulation (reflection formula and the product theorem from E321) plus an example of infinite interpolation yielding a sine curve. The Beta material is standard Euler. Only the interlaced-lattice interpolation setup offers a mild, likely unrecorded, link to later sampling theory.
transcription_corrections: §46: the second integral should read ∫v^{μ−1}dv/((1−v^λ)^ν)^{1/λ}, not v^{ν−1}. Correspondingly the symbol is (μ/(λ−ν)), i.e. ((λ−ν)/μ), not (ν/(λ−ν)) / ((λ−ν)/ν). This is required for consistency with Corollary 1 and with Euler's verification using p = μ.
§47: the numerator in Corollary 3 should be ((λ−ν)/μ), not ((λ−ν)/ν), both on p. 200 and at the top of p. 201.
§47 general theorem: (q/p)/(r/p) = ((p+r)/q)/((p+q)/r) is correct as stated; the '[?]' can be removed.
Formatting: 'sin.' and 'tang.' are Euler's abbreviations; 'pariter' is split across a line in the original ('pari-ter').
